## Methods

Data collection and pre-processing
The groundwater quality data were obtained from published articles by searching in China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI) and Web of Science. Initially, a total of 31,535 studies comprising 25,200 articles in Chinese and 6335 articles in English were retrieved using the following search formula: “Groundwater quality” (Topic) and “China” (Topic). Given the heterogeneity of the data, the retrieved publications were further filtered according to the following rules: (i) at least five groundwater quality indicators were determined; (ii) sampling locations were provided at prefecture level; (iii) there were more than five sampling points and sufficient statistical information (including mean at least); (iv) land-use type was provided; (v) samples were taken between 1990 and 2020. To effectively capture the contemporary groundwater quality status, data predating 1990 were deliberately omitted due to its limited representativeness and inadequacy in reflecting the prevailing conditions. Finally, 753 articles were identified to establish our dataset, which contains a total of 1977 surveys, as shown in Fig. S1.

The groundwater quality data were classified into two categories: non-PGQ and PGQ, based on the criteria outlined in the Groundwater Quality Standards of the People’s Republic of China (GB/T 14848-2017)22. This classification process involves the following four steps:
Step 1: Collect all relevant groundwater quality indicators from the dataset, ensuring they contain more than five indicators, as specified by established testing standards.
Step 2: Assess each indicator individually by classifying it as Class V or not, based on Table S1.
Step 3: Determine the overall groundwater quality with the worst indicator.
Step 4: Categorize the groundwater quality into two types: non-PGQ (Class I to IV) and PGQ (Class V).

In our analysis, we meticulously built the relationship between predictors and groundwater quality category (PGQ or non-PGQ). As listed in Table S2, the predictors included two classes of steady-state factors (soil properties and geographic and hydrogeologic characteristics) and four classes of time-variant factors (i.e., climate change, pollution discharge, groundwater exploitation, and land-use change).

Groundwater quality is influenced by various environmental and chemical processes, including redox reactions, contaminant transport, and natural filtration mechanisms51. Given China’s vast and diverse landscape, along with notable regional variations in data availability and quality, we prioritized accessible and quantifiable predictors to ensure broader applicability and consistency in groundwater quality predictions across different regions. Accordingly, we selected predictors that not only capture redox-related influences indirectly but also reflect other critical mechanisms affecting groundwater quality, providing a comprehensive foundation for reliable assessment. To effectively capture these complex processes, we selected predictors such as soil properties (e.g., porosity, permeability, soil type, and soil composition across different soil layers) to reflect contaminant adsorption and biological degradation, geographic and hydrogeologic characteristics (e.g., topographic wetness index, water-table ratio, and groundwater type) to indicate contaminant accumulation and natural dilution, and climatic factors (e.g., temperature, precipitation, and aridity) to represent groundwater recharge, evaporation, and pollutant mobility17,19,30. Additionally, pollution discharge (agricultural, industrial, and domestic sources) can substantially affect groundwater quality by increasing contaminant loads, while land-use change, can disrupt the natural infiltration and recharge processes52. Notably, groundwater exploitation (e.g., groundwater supply and groundwater exploitation rate) emerges as a crucial anthropogenic perturbation factor53,54. Excessive groundwater extraction lowers water tables, concentrates contaminants, and, in coastal areas, can trigger seawater intrusion, increasing salinity35,55,56. It can also mobilize naturally occurring contaminants like arsenic and fluoride, further degrading water quality30.

To classify groundwater quality at the prefecture level, we implemented a series of data preprocessing steps. First, regional data were converted into 1 km² grid cells based on regional land-use types, with all cells within a prefecture assigned the corresponding groundwater quality data to ensure consistency. The groundwater quality data were then binarized, assigning a value of zero to non-PGQ and one to PGQ. The purpose of this approach was twofold: (i) to prioritize the fundamental health aspect of safety (non-PGQ) or unsafety (PGQ) of groundwater for drinking; and (ii) to address variations in precision resulting from diverse analysis methods employed in different data sources. Next, natural factors in the predictors were extracted at a 1 km² resolution, assigning each grid cell a unique value representing local environmental conditions. Socio-economic factors were uniformly applied to all grid cells within a province, based on the sampling year. The dataset on land-use types covers specific benchmark years: 1980, 1990, 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, and every five years between 2020 and 2100. For other years, land-use data are assumed to be identical to the adjacent prior benchmark year. For instance, land-use data in 1989 are taken to be the same as those in 1980. For other dynamic factors, their cumulative average values from 1980 to the target year were calculated as the model inputs. This accounts for the lag in pollutant migration and effectively captures the long-term impacts on groundwater quality. Fertilizer consumption and pesticide consumption were averagely allocated per km2 of agricultural land, with non-agricultural land assigned zero. Industrial wastewater discharge, industrial solid waste discharge, domestic wastewater discharge, domestic solid waste discharge, and groundwater supply were allocated per km2 based on population density for each province. Per capita data for these variables were calculated by dividing the total value by the population of each province, then distributed per km2 based on population density. Groundwater exploitation rates were uniformly distributed across each province, with regions having a population density below 1 person/km² assigned a rate of zero. Other factors were allocated per km2 based on the resolution of raster data or vector data. Finally, groundwater quality categories for each year and region were matched with the corresponding natural and socio-economic variables to create the training and validation datasets for the RF model.

Model development and evaluation
In this study, the RF model was constructed to predict the spatio-temporal dynamic of groundwater quality from natural and social-economic factors. The RF model was chosen for its ability to handle large datasets with numerous predictor variables while efficiently capturing complex interactions among them24. The RF model uses the bootstrap resampling method to build multiple decision trees. For the construction of each tree, samples are independently selected; however, the distributions for all trees in the forest are the same, which guarantees the robustness of the model. In addition, the RF model offers key advantages such as preventing overfitting by introducing randomness at each decision node, which enhances generalization. By selecting random feature subsets for each tree, RF effectively addresses the challenges of high dimensionality in the data. It also reduces experimental noise and improves prediction accuracy through an ensemble approach, averaging predictions from multiple decision trees. Furthermore, RF provides inherent feature importance measures, helping identify key variables, and handles missing data efficiently, either through imputation or splitting based on available features. With minimal parameter tuning required compared to other machine learning algorithms, RF presents itself as an ideal model for this study14,57,58.

We began by optimizing the hyperparameters of the RF model, with a particular focus on the number of decision trees. By systematically testing tree counts in increments of 10, from 10 to 200, we identified 50 trees as the optimal balance between accuracy and computational efficiency (Fig. S21). Other parameters, such as minimum leaf size, were kept at their default settings, as these have proven effective in similar applications.

To further validate the model’s performance and safeguard against overfitting, we conducted 10-fold cross-validation. The dataset was randomly partitioned into 10 subsets, with 9 used for training and 1 for validation in each iteration. This process was repeated across all subsets, ensuring comprehensive evaluations. The averaged performance metrics (Table S4 and Fig. S22) confirmed the model’s ability to generalize effectively, without overfitting.

After confirming the model’s robustness through cross-validation, we proceeded to retrain it using 90% of the data (1779 surveys, comprising 67,315 points) for training and 10% (198 surveys, comprising 15,335 points) for validation, each preserving the proportion of PGQ and non-PGQ of the full dataset. This approach maximizes the model’s learning capacity by providing a larger training set while preserving an independent validation set to assess performance on unseen data. This final validation confirmed that the model maintained strong predictive accuracy, further enhancing its generalization ability.

To precisely and comprehensively establish the relationship between model predictors and groundwater quality, 51 predictor variables were initially included. We conducted Pearson correlation analysis to reduce redundancy in the predictor variables. Initially, all original variables were included in the RF model training. Among the list of candidate variables, one is opted out if its Pearson correlation coefficient23 with any other variables was larger than 0.7. However, certain variables were retained despite exceeding this correlation threshold. This decision was made given that excluding these variables notably reduced the model’s predictive performance, demonstrating their essential contributions to accurately capturing the system’s dynamics. This step-by-step approach ensures that the final set of variables used in modeling or further analysis is less likely to include redundant information, thus improving the parsimony and interpretability of the model. Finally, 25 predictors were reserved to predict the groundwater quality in China. The data sources and detailed information about these predictors were described in the Supplementary Information.

The final RF model was trained with 50 trees using the selected 25 predictors as inputs to classify each 1 km2 grid as being PGQ or not. Each decision tree in the forest casts a ‘vote’ for a class label based on the input data, with the final class label determined by the majority vote across all trees. The model also calculates class-label probabilities based on the proportion of trees voting for each class. The performance of the RF model is systematically validated with the following metrics.

Prevalence (Prev) quantifies the proportion of actual positives in the dataset and is calculated as follows59:
Prev = (TP+FN) / (TP+FN+TN+FP) (1)

where TP (true positives) are samples correctly identified as PGQ; FN (false negatives) are samples incorrectly identified as non-PGQ; TN (true negatives) are samples correctly identified as non-PGQ; FP (false positives) are samples incorrectly identified as PGQ.

General statistical indices, such as accuracy (Acc), sensitivity (Sen), precision (Prec) and specificity (Spec), were employed to quantify the bias of the RF model, with higher values indicating better model effectiveness60. The definitions of TP, TN, FP, and FN shed light on the seemingly subtle distinctions among these statistics, which play a crucial role in assessing the model’s performance and its ability to minimize false positives and negatives59:

Acc = (TP+TN) / (TP+FN+TN+FP) (2)

Sen = TP / (TP+FN) (3)

Prec = TP / (TP+FP) (4)

Spec = TN / (TN+FP) (5)

The performance of the trained RF model was then assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC). The ROC curve is primarily used to evaluate the performance of a classification model by showing the trade-off between the sensitivity and specificity across different thresholds61. AUC is a single measure that summarizes the overall performance of RF for classification. The higher the AUC, the better the model is at distinguishing between PGQ and non-PGQ. A perfect classifier would have an AUC of 1, while a completely random one would have an AUC of 0.5.

Additionally, Cohen’s kappa coefficient (K), which measures the agreement between the observed and predicted classifications corrected for chance, is used to further assess the model’s accuracy59. Kappa coefficient of 0.6–0.8 is generally considered good, and values above 0.8 are deemed excellent, calculated by:

K = (Po - Pe) / (1 - Pe) (6)

where Po is the observed agreement (Acc), and Pe is the expected agreement by chance:

Pe = ((TP+FP) * (TP+FN) + (FN+TN) * (FP+TN)) / (TP+FN+TN+FP)^2 (7)

Apart from evaluating the predictive abilities of the RF model, the spatial patterns of the estimates were validated by comparing them with nationally recognized maps, ensuring their consistency and reliability.

To assess predictor importance, we utilized the error of out-of-bag (OOB) samples among trees, a common metric employed in RF models. This approach involves randomly permuting the values of a specific predictor variable and calculating the resulting change in OOB error. OOB error refers to the prediction error computed on samples that were not included in the bootstrap sample used to train each decision tree in the RF model. If permuting a predictor leads to a considerable increase in OOB error, it suggests that the variable plays a critical role in prediction accuracy. This approach offers a reliable means of identifying the important features for model prediction.

To further assess the sensitivity of each influencing factor on the model’s predictions62, we conducted a sensitivity analysis by systematically increasing or decreasing each continuous predictor by 10%. This approach allowed us to observe how these perturbations influenced the predicted average probability of PGQ over the historical period from 1980 to 2020. By comparing these modified predictions to the baseline scenario, where no changes to the predictors were applied, we were able to quantify the degree to which each factor contributed to variability in PGQ probability, providing insights into which predictors most notably affect groundwater quality predictions under different conditions.

Following the identification of key predictors, partial dependence plots (PDPs) were generated to visualize each predictor’s marginal effect on the probability of PGQ. The PDPs were generated by holding the focal predictor constant across its empirical range while integrating out the effects of all other predictors, thereby isolating the unique contribution of the predictor to the response63. This was achieved by averaging the model predictions over the distribution of the data, providing a clear visual representation of the dependency between the predictors and the probability of PGQ.

In addition, feature interaction charts (FICs) were constructed to explore the combined effect of two predictors on the predicted probability of PGQ63. It takes into account the range of values for the two concerned predictors. However, instead of holding one variable constant, FICs vary both variables simultaneously over their empirical ranges. The model’s predictions are then averaged over the joint distribution of the two predictors, and the combined effect is visualized in a two-dimensional color-coded map. This approach highlights how the interaction between two predictors influences the model output, thus providing a deeper understanding of the relationships within the data.

PGQ prediction
The RF model was used to reconstruct and predict the spatiotemporal distribution of groundwater quality from 1980 to 2100, enabling us to infer long-term trends in populations potentially exposed to PGQ. We apply a probability cutoff (Prob_cut) of 0.5 to identify the populations at risk in areas exceeding this threshold. Then the affected population living in each grid (1 km2) was calculated by multiplying the grid’s population (Pop) by its probability of PGQ (Prob_poor). The calculation of the potentially affected population (Pop_affect) is summarized in the following equations:

Pop_affect = Pop * Prob_poor, Prob_poor > Prob_cut (8)
Pop_affect = 0, Prob_poor <= Prob_cut

The dynamics of PGQ probability among different periods were controlled by the four categories of time-variant drivers (i.e., climate change, pollution discharge, groundwater exploitation, and land-use change). To quantify the contribution of each driver on PGQ, we designed factorial experiments between 1980 and 2020. In the experiment, we just kept one specific driver category (e.g., climate) constant at their initial states in 1980, while allowing the other driver categories vary with time as they are (i.e., the time series in the real world). For instance, the Prob_Climate means that all drivers in the climate category remained constant at values in 1980 but with real (time-variant) features of drivers in pollution and groundwater categories.

By comparing the simulations between experiments, we could isolate the impact of a target driver category and quantify its contribution. To implement the comparison, we defined the differences between simulation driven by all variables in period y (Prob_All,y) and that driven by partial time-variant driver categories (Prob_Vi,y) as the actual contribution of the target variable i (Vi) and period y (Con_Vi,y):

Con_Vi,y = Prob_All,y - Prob_Vi,y (9)

The relative contribution (%) of variable i (i=1, 2, 3,…, n) and period y (y=1, 2, 3,…, k) (RelCon_Vi,y) was defined as:

RelCon_Vi,y = |Con_Vi,y| / sum(|Con_Vi,y|) * 100% (10)

To quantify the contribution of each driver category to changes in PGQ area ratio on the national scale, we define the differences between the area ratio of PGQ driven by all variables in period y (AR_All,y) and that driven by partial time-variant driver categories (AR_Vi,y) as the primitive contribution of the target variable i (Vi) and period y (ConAR_Vi,y):

ConAR_Vi,y = AR_All,y - AR_Vi,y (11)

The differences between the area ratio of PGQ driven by all variables in period y (AR_All,y) and that driven by all variables in the baseline year (AR_All,BY) are defined as the actual growth:

ActAR_All,y = AR_All,y - AR_All,BY (12)

Then, the relative contributions of each driver category to changes in the PGQ area ratio are calculated as:

RelAR_Vi,y = (ConAR_Vi,y / sum(ConAR_Vi,y)) * ActAR_All,y (13)

The grid annual mean relative contributions of the four driver categories in groundwater were used to visualize the spatial patterns of the influential intensity of different driver categories on a national scale. We defined the single dominant driver category of each pixel as the variable with a maximum relative contribution. As pollution discharges are composed of agricultural, industrial, and domestic pollution, the dominant driver category of pollution discharge for each pixel is defined as the secondary driver category with the largest relative contributions among the three secondary driver categories.

To further elucidate the temporal dynamics of groundwater quality, the differences in the projected groundwater quality categories for the years 2020, 2000, and 1980 were calculated, generating maps of groundwater quality changes for the periods 1980–2000, 2000–2020, and 1980–2020. Regions of groundwater quality deterioration (non-PGQ to PGQ) during these periods were extracted as masks. This approach yielded detailed maps of the driving factors behind deteriorated groundwater quality regions across the three distinct periods.

In future scenarios, the analysis of dominant driver focuses exclusively on four primary categories: climate change, groundwater exploitation, land use and pollution discharges, without individually detailing secondary pollution categories. We kept one specific driver category (e.g., climate) constant at its states in 2020, while allowing the other driver categories to vary with time.

We evaluated the temporal evolution of groundwater quality from 2021 to 2100 in four different scenarios, which allowed us to assess the long-term changes in groundwater quality by considering the continuity of the underlying factors over the specified time frame. To evaluate the impacts of climate change on groundwater quality, we utilized the SSP scenarios, namely SSP1-1.9, SSP2-4.5, and SSP5-8.5, as outlined in the IPCC AR664. These scenarios provide a framework for understanding and projecting different socio-economic and climate conditions, allowing us to examine the potential responses of groundwater quality to various development and climate change trajectories.

In Scenario I (Baseline), we assumed a consistent development intensity for all drivers. Climate, groundwater exploitation, and pollution discharges were maintained at the same levels as the cumulative average values in 2020. Similarly, land-use type in Scenario I was also assumed to remain unchanged from 2020. In contrast, Scenarios II-IV incorporated projections to account for future variability. Specifically, climate data from one CMIP6 model—EC-Earth3 were used as model input to project future PGQ probabilities65–67. Additionally, land-use data in these scenarios were derived from the SSP-RCP global 1km land-use simulation dataset (2020-2100) for SSP1-1.9, SSP2-4.5, and SSP5-8.5 scenarios, updated every five years68. To maintain consistency in representation, these land-use data were aligned with those used for the historical period from 1980 to 2020.

In the three scenarios, annual change rates of −3%, 1%, and 3% were assigned as gradients for groundwater exploitation and pollution discharge, respectively. These rates were determined based on historical trends69,70 and future projections71,72 related to industrial activities, agricultural expansion, and environmental policies. The low rate of −3% reflects a proactive approach toward reducing resource use and pollution discharge, aligning with the sustainability-focused SSP1-1.9 scenario73. In contrast, the medium rate of 1% corresponds to a moderate development pathway, as seen in SSP2-4.5. This scenario embodies a balanced approach, allowing socio-economic development to progress while placing emphasis on environmental protection74. The high rate of 3% aligns with the SSP5-8.5 scenario, characterized by rapid economic growth and minimal environmental regulation75. The scenarios thus represent a spectrum of future development and industrial expansion. We acknowledge that future development may exhibit more intricate patterns, and our current study may not fully capture this complexity and uncertainty. Then, these rates were applied to the corresponding values from 2021 to 2100, and the cumulative average was calculated as the model inputs for each year. Please refer to Table S5 for detailed information on the specific scenario assumptions.

To evaluate the impact of uncertainties in climate change, groundwater exploitation, and pollution charge on model predictions, we applied Monte Carlo (MC) simulations to quantify the variability in groundwater quality predictions due to input uncertainties76. This analysis was conducted for the period 1980–2100, with data processed at 5-year intervals for 1980–2015, annually from 2016 to 2020, and at 5-year intervals for future projections from 2025 to 2100 under four scenarios.

In each scenario-year combination, MC simulations with 50 members were run to introduce variability in key natural and socio-economic predictors. Perturbations were applied to these dominant factors, such as climate, groundwater exploitation and pollution charge, reflecting their real-world uncertainties. For instance, temperature varied within a ±2°C range, while predictors like precipitation, fertilizer, and pesticide use were perturbed by up to ±20%.

The results of these simulations can be used to evaluate the range of possible groundwater quality outcomes based on uncertainties in input data. For each year and scenario, we calculated the mean and standard deviation of the predicted probabilities based on the ensemble outcomes, providing a robust estimate of both expectation and variability in groundwater quality predictions.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

This paper addresses a critical environmental issue, exploring the groundwater quality crisis across China using extensive data and Random Forest (RF) modeling technique. The study is well-motivated and holds significant implications for environmental management and policy-making. The manuscript is generally well-structured, with a clear introduction, and comprehensive results and discussion sections. However, there are several areas where the manuscript could be strengthened to enhance its clarity, robustness, and impact. Specifically, the methodology section needs more detail on the hyperparameter tuning process, data preprocessing steps, and the rationale for choosing the RF model. Additionally, the results section would benefit from a more detailed interpretation of the key predictors and a thorough uncertainty assessment in the scenario analysis. Finally, the discussion should provide a more nuanced analysis of the interactions between various drivers of groundwater quality and offer specific policy recommendations based on the study's findings. Addressing these areas will significantly improve the manuscript's scientific rigor and practical relevance.
Major concerns:
1) The current methodology provides limited details on the hyperparameter tuning process for the Random Forest (RF) model. Specifically, it lacks a thorough explanation of how the number of trees, maximum depth, and other critical parameters were optimized. Elaborate on the hyperparameter tuning process by describing the specific methods used, such as grid search or randomized search. Include a discussion on the range of values tested for each parameter, the criteria for selecting the optimal values, and any cross-validation techniques employed to ensure robust model performance. For instance, detailing the grid search process might include explaining the range of the number of trees tested (e.g., 50 to 500 in increments of 50), the range of maximum depth (e.g., 5 to 30), and the evaluation metric used to select the best combination (e.g., highest AUC score on validation sets). Additionally, explain how overfitting was addressed, such as by using cross-validation techniques and evaluating the model on a separate validation set to ensure it generalizes well to unseen data.
Discuss the rationale for selecting the RF model over other machine learning algorithms, emphasizing its strengths in handling large datasets with numerous predictor variables and its ability to capture complex interactions between predictors without requiring extensive parameter tuning. ### Reviewer 2

The study of groundwater quality evolution is of significant importance and relevance, given its pivotal role in sustaining freshwater resources and maintaining ecosystem health. The application of machine learning, particularly the random forest model, to analyze and predict the spatiotemporal dynamics of groundwater quality across entire China is innovative and represents a valuable contribution to the field. The manuscript is well organized and easy to follow. However, there are several areas that require clarification and additional detail to enhance the robustness and transparency of this study. Below are some comments and suggestions aimed at improving the manuscript:
1. Definition of Poor Groundwater Quality (PGQ): The study does not clearly distinguish between PGQ caused by human activities and that resulting from geogenic origins, two distinct categories influenced by different driving forces. Moreover, different groundwater pollutants have different sources and influencing factors. For example, nitrogen pollution from non-point sources is significantly affected by surface input and migration through the unsaturated zone, yet the machine learning model does not account for the impact of the unsaturated zone. Similarly, heavy metals are largely influenced by redox conditions, especially in cases where naturally poor-quality groundwater is more affected by hydrogeological conditions than by surface processes. Consequently, the machine learning model may overemphasize the role of surface soil, potentially overlooking other critical factors.
2. Hydrogeological Factors: While this study developed a machine learning model to construct annual probabilistic maps of poor groundwater quality across China using 25 natural and social-economic factors, few of these are explicitly related to hydrogeological processes. Groundwater flow and solute transport are clearly significant for predicting groundwater quality. As an example, the authors mention a factor called 'Aquifer-media-based groundwater type' in the supporting information, but its establishment is not clearly explained. Does this refer to distinctions such as confined vs. unconfined, porous media vs fractured media, or other characteristics?
3. Chemical Processes: As noted in comment #1, chemical processes is critical in determining groundwater quality. For example, nitrate (NO3), one of the indicators considered in this study for groundwater quality, is redox-sensitive and undergoes denitrification under reducing conditions. Nitrate concentrations in groundwater are therefore strongly dependent on redox conditions, regardless of nitrogen input at the land surface. How redox conditions are considered in assessing the groundwater quality is an area that warrants further exploration.
4. Temporal Variations: This study aims to investigate the temporal changes in Chinese groundwater quality; however, only social-economic factors were considered temporally dynamic, while soil and environmental factors were treated steady-state. It’s noteworthy that environmental conditions vary over time, especially the depth to the water table, which in turn affects contaminant transport from the land surface to the underlying aquifer system. Considering these factors as steady state may underestimate their impacts, and this should be addressed in the paper.
5. Data Set Clarity: The manuscript mentions the number of surveys derived from a certain number of articles but does not specify the exact number of data points within the groundwater quality dataset. For clarity, could you please provide the total number of data points and detail how they are divided into training and validation sets? This information is crucial for understanding the scale of the analysis and the potential for model overfitting.
6. Spatial Partitioning Methodology (L.365-372): The method of spatial partitioning into 1KM*1KM grids requires further elaboration. Specifically, it is unclear how the presence of both PGQ and non-PGQ within a single grid is resolved. Additionally, please elucidate how point-scale driver variables are expanded to fit the 1KM*1KM grid format. A clear explanation of these methodologies will greatly aid in understanding the spatial analysis performed.
7. Model Parameters and Tuning: The manuscript would benefit from a detailed description of the random forest model parameters, including the settings for each parameter and the methods used for tuning. If parameter optimization was conducted, please describe the process and the rationale behind the chosen methods and settings.
8. Uncertainty Analysis: An uncertainty analysis of the model results would be beneficial. Providing an assessment of the model’s uncertainty will give readers a better understanding of the reliability of the predictions.
9. Data Processing Details: It would be beneficial to include a section on data preprocessing. Specifically, readers would benefit from knowing whether the input driver variable data were standardized or normalized before being fed into the model. Standardization is a common practice in machine learning to ensure that each feature contributes proportionately to the final prediction.
10. Rationale for future scenario settings (L.497-514): The setting of future scenarios is crucial for the interpretation of model results. Given that variables such as fertilizer and pesticide usage appear to have a significant impact on the model, as indicated by Fig. S3 and the results section, the rationale behind the high (3%), medium (1%), and low (-3%) annual change rates should be discussed. This discussion could include the basis for these specific rates and how they align with projected socio-economic and environmental trends.
Addressing these points will significantly improve the manuscript and provide readers with a clearer understanding of your research methodology and findings.

(1) In the revised manuscript, we have provided a more detailed explanation of the scenario construction
process in “Scenario settings” section of “Methods”, outlining the data sources, underlying assumptions,
and adjustments made for future projections:
“In Scenario I (Baseline), we assumed a consistent development intensity for all drivers.
Climate, groundwater exploitation, and pollution discharges were maintained at the same
levels as the cumulative average values in 2020. Similarly, land-use type in Scenario I was
also assumed to remain unchanged from 2020. In contrast, Scenarios II-IV incorporated
projections to account for future variability. Specifically, climate data from one CMIP6
model——EC-Earth3 were used as model input to project future PGQ probabilities65-67.
Additionally, land-use data in these scenarios were derived from the SSP-RCP global 1km
land-use simulation dataset (2020-2100) for SSP1-1.9, SSP2-4.5, and SSP5-8.5 scenarios,
updated every five years68. To maintain consistency in representation, these land-use data were
aligned with those used for the historical period from 1980 to 2020.
In the three scenarios, annual change rates of -3%, 1%, and 3% were assigned as gradients
for groundwater exploitation and pollution discharge, respectively. These rates were
determined based on historical trends69,70 and future projections71,72 related to industrial
activities, agricultural expansion, and environmental policies. The low rate of -3% reflects a
proactive approach toward reducing resource use and pollution discharge, aligning with the
sustainability-focused SSP1-1.9 scenario73. In contrast, the medium rate of 1% corresponds
to a moderate development pathway, as seen in SSP2-4.5. This scenario embodies a balanced
approach, allowing socio-economic development to progress while placing emphasis on
environmental protection74. The high rate of 3% aligns with the SSP5-8.5 scenario,
characterized by rapid economic growth and minimal environmental regulation75. This
scenario anticipates high energy demands, with significant reliance on fossil fuels and
industrial expansion. We acknowledge that future development may exhibit more intricate
patterns, and our current study may not fully capture this complexity and uncertainty. Then,
these rates were applied to the corresponding values from 2021 to 2100, and the cumulative
average was calculated as the model inputs in each year. Please refer to Table S5 for detailed
information on the specific scenario assumptions.”

(2) To evaluate the impact of uncertainties in climate, groundwater exploitation, and pollution data on
model predictions, we conducted Monte Carlo simulations using n=50 sets of randomized input data
representing various uncertain future scenarios. This approach enables us to quantify output uncertainty
and highlight the range of possible outcomes and their implications. By incorporating these uncertainty
assessments, we offer a clearer understanding of potential future groundwater quality under different
conditions, providing policymakers with valuable insights into associated risks.
We have detailed the steps and methods used for uncertainty analysis in the “Uncertainty analysis”
section of “Methods”:
“Uncertainty analysis
To evaluate the impact of uncertainties in climate change, groundwater exploitation, and
pollution charge on model predictions, we applied Monte Carlo (MC) simulations to quantify
the variability in groundwater quality predictions due to input uncertainties76. This analysis
was conducted for the period 1980-2100, with data processed at 5-year intervals for 1980-
2015, annually from 2016 to 2020, and at 5-year intervals for future projections from 2025 to
2100 under four scenarios.
In each scenario-year combination, MC simulations with 50 members were run to introduce
variability in key natural and socio-economic predictors. Perturbations were applied to these
dominant factors, such as climate, groundwater exploitation and pollution charge, reflecting
their real-world uncertainties. For instance, temperature varied within a ±2°C range, while
predictors like precipitation, fertilizer, and pesticide use were perturbed by up to ±20%.
The results of these simulations can be used to evaluate the range of possible groundwater
quality outcomes based on uncertainties in input data. For each year and scenario, we
calculated the mean and standard deviation of the predicted probabilities based on the
ensemble outcomes, providing a robust estimate of both expectation and variability in
groundwater quality predictions.”
In addition, we have included an uncertainty analysis in “Discussion”:
“Although visual comparisons and statistical evaluations suggest that the model estimates are
generally reasonable, notable uncertainties remain. Monte Carlo simulations were used to
assess uncertainties in PGQ probability predictions, providing insights into spatial and
temporal variability. As shown in Fig. S18(d-f) and Fig. S19(e-h), uncertainties are moderate
overall but higher in North and Northeast China from 1980 to 2100, likely due to socio-
economic variability and complex groundwater interactions. Under Scenario IV,
uncertainties become more pronounced (Fig. S20), likely driven by increased emissions and groundwater
exploitation. This highlights the need for adaptive groundwater management strategies,
particularly in high-emission scenarios, to mitigate adverse impacts and enhance prediction
reliability in vulnerable regions.”

“In this study, our model ranks the factors that significantly influence the prediction accuracy
of groundwater quality, identifying depth-based groundwater type as the most critical
predictor (Fig. S3). Sensitivity analysis, involving a ±10% change in each variable,
highlighted permeability as the most sensitive factor (Fig. S13). In addition, we analyzed the
interrelationships among the predictors (Fig. S2), as well as the partial dependence plots and
feature interaction charts (Fig. S14 and S15), demonstrating the complex interactions among
the predictors. Shallow groundwater is more vulnerable to surface contaminants, while deeper
groundwater is less impacted27. Regions with lower precipitation, higher temperatures, and
higher groundwater exploitation rates showed higher PGQ probabilities (Fig. S15). Climate-
driven changes directly affect recharge rates, influence groundwater replenishment, while
indirectly alter groundwater usage patterns28. In arid and semi-arid regions, reduced rainfall
leads to over-extraction and higher pollutant concentrations due to decreased dilution,
whereas humid regions see increased mobilization and dilution of pollutants29-30. As climate
change continues to reshape global temperature and precipitation patterns, these dynamics
are expected to become increasingly complex. Additionally, soil sand content (100-200 cm)
significantly affects recharge and contamination, with higher content increasing susceptibility
to surface contaminants (Fig. S14f)31. It is essential to note that this analysis is based on a
nationwide perspective, and the most critical predictors vary spatially, as shown in Fig. S7a.
These insights highlight the importance of informing policymakers and stakeholders about
region-specific factors that must be managed to improve groundwater quality.”

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The study of groundwater quality evolution is of significant importance and relevance, given its pivotal
role in sustaining freshwater resources and maintaining ecosystem health. The application of machine
learning, particularly the random forest model, to analyze and predict the spatiotemporal dynamics of
groundwater quality across entire China is innovative and represents a valuable contribution to the field.
The manuscript is well organized and easy to follow. However, there are several areas that require
clarification and additional detail to enhance the robustness and transparency of this study. Below are
some comments and suggestions aimed at improving the manuscript:
1. Definition of Poor Groundwater Quality (PGQ): The study does not clearly distinguish between
PGQ caused by human activities and that resulting from geogenic origins, two distinct categories
influenced by different driving forces. Moreover, different groundwater pollutants have different
sources and influencing factors. For example, nitrogen pollution from non-point sources is
significantly affected by surface input and migration through the unsaturated zone, yet the
machine learning model does not account for the impact of the unsaturated zone. Similarly, heavy
metals are largely influenced by redox conditions, especially in cases where naturally poor-quality
groundwater is more affected by hydrogeological conditions than by surface processes.
Consequently, the machine learning model may overemphasize the role of surface soil, potentially
overlooking other critical factors.
Response: Thank you for your valuable feedback on the definition of PGQ and the potential limitations
of our approach.
(1) Our study defines PGQ based on the latest Chinese groundwater quality standards, classifying
groundwater as either poor or not poor for drinking purposes. Since the original groundwater quality data
collected from the literature lacks explicit information about contamination sources, we were unable to
clearly differentiate between PGQ caused by human activities and geogenic factors when training the
model. However, we examined the spatial distribution of the dominant drivers of groundwater quality
changes across China, as shown in Fig. S7(a). This analysis provides a rough distinction between PGQ
driven by anthropogenic activities and that arising from natural processes.
In the revised manuscript, we have added the following text to “Discussion” to acknowledge the
limitations of our approach:
“Furthermore, the lack of distinction between geogenic and anthropogenic sources of PGQ
and depth differentiation among phreatic, confined, and unspecified groundwater samples
could affect the accuracy of predictions.”

(2) Additionally, we recognize that different pollutants come from distinct sources and are influenced by
various factors, with hydrogeological processes being just as important as surface processes. To address
this, our machine learning model integrates subsurface factors alongside surface soil characteristics. For
example, we incorporate soil properties at depths of 100-200 cm and account for various groundwater
types based on aquifer media, such as pore water in loose sediments, karst water in carbonate rocks, and
fissure water in igneous and metamorphic rocks (Table S2). This approach ensures that deeper
hydrogeological influences are adequately considered without overemphasizing surface soil factors.
In the revised manuscript, we have clarified the principle of predictor collection in the “Predictor
collection and pre-processing” section of “Methods”:
“In our analysis, we meticulously built the relationship between predictors and groundwater
quality category (PGQ or non-PGQ). As listed in Table S2, the predictors included two classes
of steady-state factors (soil properties and geographic and hydrogeologic characteristics) and
four classes of time-variant factors (i.e., climate change, pollution discharge, groundwater
exploitation, and land-use change).
Groundwater quality is influenced by various environmental and chemical processes,
including redox reactions, contaminant transport, and natural filtration mechanisms51. Given
China’s vast and diverse landscape, along with significant regional variations in data
availability and quality, we prioritized accessible and quantifiable predictors to ensure
broader applicability and consistency in groundwater quality predictions across different
regions. Accordingly, we selected predictors that not only capture redox-related influences
indirectly but also reflect other critical mechanisms affecting groundwater quality, providing
a comprehensive foundation for reliable assessment. To effectively capture these complex
processes, we selected predictors such as soil properties (e.g., porosity, permeability, soil type,
and soil composition across different soil layers) to reflect contaminant adsorption and
biological degradation, geographic and hydrogeologic characteristics (e.g., topographic
wetness index, water-table ratio, and groundwater type) to indicate contaminant accumulation
and natural dilution, and climatic factors (e.g., temperature, precipitation, and aridity) to
represent groundwater recharge, evaporation, and pollutant mobility17,19,29. Additionally,
pollution discharge (agricultural, industrial, and domestic sources) can significantly affect
groundwater quality by increasing contaminant loads, while land-use change, can disrupt the
natural infiltration and recharge processes52. Notably, groundwater exploitation (e.g.,
groundwater supply and groundwater exploitation rate) emerges as a crucial anthropogenic
perturbation factor53,54. Excessive groundwater extraction lowers water tables, concentrates
contaminants, and, in coastal areas, can trigger seawater intrusion, increasing salinity34,55,56.
It can also mobilize naturally occurring contaminants like arsenic and fluoride, further
degrading water quality29.”

3. Chemical Processes: As noted in comment #1, chemical processes are critical in determining
groundwater quality. For example, nitrate (NO3), one of the indicators considered in this study for
groundwater quality, is redox-sensitive and undergoes denitrification under reducing conditions.
Nitrate concentrations in groundwater are therefore strongly dependent on redox conditions,
regardless of nitrogen input at the land surface. How redox conditions are considered in assessing
the groundwater quality is an area that warrants further exploration.
Response: Thank you for your insightful comment. In response to your observation regarding the role
of chemical processes, particularly redox conditions, in determining groundwater quality, we would like
to clarify the following:
(1) We fully acknowledge the significant role redox conditions play in shaping groundwater quality,
especially for redox-sensitive indicators like nitrate. While our model does not explicitly include a redox
potential variable, certain predictors—such as climate conditions, soil properties, and groundwater
types—indirectly capture variations that influence denitrification and other redox-related processes.
(2) We recognize that redox potential is particularly crucial for pollutants like heavy metals, which are
sensitive to these conditions. However, many groundwater quality indicators are less impacted by redox
potential. Our model prioritizes factors that affect a broad range of indicators, as outlined in the latest
Chinese groundwater quality standards, rather than focusing exclusively on contaminants sensitive to
redox changes. Additionally, the limited availability and consistency of redox data across China led us
to focus on more accessible and quantifiable factors.
(3) We emphasize that our study operates on a large national scale with a spatial resolution of 1 km²,
which restricts the ability to capture fine-scale biochemical processes, such as site-specific denitrification.
Such processes require high-resolution data for accurate representation, which is beyond the scope of
this study. Therefore, we relied on indirect predictors that can capture these processes at a broader scale.
In the revised manuscript, we have added the following text to clarify these points:
Discussion:
“Lastly, our model prioritizes factors influencing overall groundwater quality rather than
specific indicators, potentially differing from more targeted assessments.”
Predictor collection and pre-processing:
“In our analysis, we meticulously built the relationship between predictors and groundwater
quality category (PGQ or non-PGQ). As listed in Table S2, the predictors included two classes
of steady-state factors (soil properties and geographic and hydrogeologic characteristics) and
four classes of time-variant factors (i.e., climate change, pollution discharge, groundwater
exploitation, and land-use change).
Groundwater quality is influenced by various environmental and chemical processes,
including redox reactions, contaminant transport, and natural filtration mechanisms51. Given
China’s vast and diverse landscape, along with significant regional variations in data
availability and quality, we prioritized accessible and quantifiable predictors to ensure
broader applicability and consistency in groundwater quality predictions across different
regions. Accordingly, we selected predictors that not only capture redox-related influences
indirectly but also reflect other critical mechanisms affecting groundwater quality, providing
a comprehensive foundation for reliable assessment. To effectively capture these complex
processes, we selected predictors such as soil properties (e.g., porosity, permeability, soil type,
and soil composition across different soil layers) to reflect contaminant adsorption and
biological degradation, geographic and hydrogeologic characteristics (e.g., topographic
wetness index, water-table ratio, and groundwater type) to indicate contaminant accumulation
and natural dilution, and climatic factors (e.g., temperature, precipitation, and aridity) to
represent groundwater recharge, evaporation, and pollutant mobility17,19,29. Additionally,
pollution discharge (agricultural, industrial, and domestic sources) can significantly affect
groundwater quality by increasing contaminant loads, while land-use change, can disrupt the
natural infiltration and recharge processes52. Notably, groundwater exploitation (e.g.,
groundwater supply and groundwater exploitation rate) emerges as a crucial anthropogenic
perturbation factor53,54. Excessive groundwater extraction lowers water tables, concentrates
contaminants, and, in coastal areas, can trigger seawater intrusion, increasing salinity34,55,56.
It can also mobilize naturally occurring contaminants like arsenic and fluoride, further
degrading water quality29.”

4. Temporal Variations: This study aims to investigate the temporal changes in Chinese
groundwater quality; however, only social-economic factors were considered temporally dynamic,
while soil and environmental factors were treated steady-state. It’s noteworthy that environmental
conditions vary over time, especially the depth to the water table, which in turn affects contaminant
transport from the land surface to the underlying aquifer system. Considering these factors as
steady state may underestimate their impacts, and this should be addressed in the paper.
Response: Thank you for the valuable suggestion. We would like to address your concern as follows:
(1) Due to limitations in the availability and validity of dynamic data for soil and hydrogeological
variables, we were unable to incorporate temporal changes for these factors directly. The lack of
consistent, high-resolution temporal data across the study period constrained our ability to model their
full dynamism. Therefore, we used available steady-state data to represent these factors within the model.
(2) To account for the influence of fluctuations in soil and environmental factors on groundwater quality
through changes in contaminant transport, we conducted a sensitivity analysis by introducing a ±10%
perturbation to these predictors. This approach helps us understand the impact of potential temporal
variability of predictors within the constraints of available data.
We have included the following text in “Discussion” to address this consideration and to acknowledge
the limitations of our approach:
“In this study, our model ranks the factors that significantly influence the prediction accuracy
of groundwater quality, identifying depth-based groundwater type as the most critical
predictor (Fig. S3). Sensitivity analysis, involving a ±10% change in each variable,
highlighted permeability as the most sensitive factor (Fig. S13).”
“Additionally, assuming steady-state conditions for environmental variables like soil
properties and water table depth may overlook key temporal variations, limiting the capture
of dynamic contaminant transport over time.”
In addition, we have detailed the steps and methods used for the sensitivity analysis in the
“Assessment of predictor importance” section of “Methods”:
“To further assess the sensitivity of each influencing factor on the model’s predictions62, we
conducted a sensitivity analysis by systematically increasing or decreasing each continuous
predictor by 10%. This approach allowed us to observe how these perturbations influenced
the predicted average probability of PGQ over the historical period from 1980 to 2020. By
comparing these modified predictions to the baseline scenario, where no changes to the
predictors were applied, we were able to quantify the degree to which each factor contributed
to variability in PGQ probability, providing insights into which predictors most significantly
affect groundwater quality predictions under different conditions.

5. Data Set Clarity: The manuscript mentions the number of surveys derived from a certain
number of articles but does not specify the exact number of data points within the groundwater
quality dataset. For clarity, could you please provide the total number of data points and detail
how they are divided into training and validation sets? This information is crucial for
understanding the scale of the analysis and the potential for model overfitting.
Response: Thank you for your suggestion. The groundwater quality dataset contains 82,650 data points
collected from 1,977 surveys. We allocated 90% of the surveys (1,779 surveys, comprising 67,315 points)
for training the RF model, and the remaining 10% (198 surveys, comprising 15,335 points) for validation.
This division ensures a balance between providing ample training data and maintaining a robust
validation process, thereby strengthening the credibility and reliability of our model’s predictions.
Although RF models are inherently resistant to overfitting, we also applied cross-validation to rigorously
assess model performance. Overfitting was not observed during these evaluations. In the revised
manuscript, we have clarified this with the following text:
“To further validate the model’s performance and safeguard against overfitting, we conducted
10-fold cross-validation. The dataset was randomly partitioned into 10 subsets, with 9 used
for training and 1 for validation in each iteration. This process was repeated across all subsets,
ensuring comprehensive evaluations. The averaged performance metrics (Table S4 and Fig.
S22) confirmed the model’s ability to generalize effectively, without overfitting.
After confirming the model’s robustness through cross-validation, we proceeded to retrain it
using 90% of the data (1,779 surveys, comprising 67,315 points) for training and 10% (198
surveys, comprising 15,335 points) for validation, each preserving the proportion of PGQ and
non-PGQ of the full dataset. This approach maximizes the model’s learning capacity by
providing a larger training set while preserving an independent validation set to assess
performance on unseen data. This final validation confirmed that the model maintained strong
predictive accuracy, further enhancing its generalization ability.”
6. Spatial Partitioning Methodology (L.365-372): The method of spatial partitioning into
1KM*1KM grids requires further elaboration. Specifically, it is unclear how the presence of both
PGQ and non-PGQ within a single grid is resolved. Additionally, please elucidate how point-scale
driver variables are expanded to fit the 1KM*1KM grid format. A clear explanation of these
methodologies will greatly aid in understanding the spatial analysis performed.
Response:Thank you for your insightful comments. We have thoroughly reviewed our original dataset
and confirmed that no instances exist where a single 1 km² grid contains both PGQ and non-PGQ
classifications. In the event such a scenario arises, the grid would be classified as PGQ, as the presence
of groundwater degradation within the grid takes precedence in determining the classification.
In the revised manuscript, we have clearly explained the process of partitioning both the predictors and
target variables into the 1 km² grids:
“To classify groundwater quality at the prefecture level, we implemented a series of data
preprocessing steps. First, regional data were converted into 1 km² grid cells based on
regional land-use types, with all cells within a prefecture assigned the corresponding
groundwater quality data to ensure consistency. The groundwater quality data were then
binarized, assigning a value of zero to non-PGQ and one to PGQ. The purpose of this
approach was twofold: (i) to prioritize the fundamental health aspect of safety (non-PGQ) or
unsafety (PGQ) of groundwater for drinking; and (ii) to address variations in precision
resulting from diverse analysis methods employed in different data sources. Next, natural
factors in the predictors were extracted at a 1 km² resolution, assigning each grid cell a unique
value representing local environmental conditions. Socio-economic factors were uniformly
applied to all grid cells within a province, based on the sampling year. The dataset on land-
use types covers specific benchmark years: 1980, 1990, 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020,
and every five years between 2020 and 2100. For other years, land-use data are assumed to
be identical to the adjacent prior benchmark year. For instance, land-use data in 1989 are
taken to be the same as those in 1980. For other dynamic factors, their cumulative average
values from 1980 to the target year were calculated as the model inputs. This accounts for the
lag in pollutant migration and effectively captures the long-term impacts on groundwater
quality. Fertilizer consumption and pesticide consumption were averagely allocated per km2
of agricultural land, with non-agricultural land assigned zero. Industrial wastewater
discharge, industrial solid waste discharge, domestic wastewater discharge, domestic solid
waste discharge, and groundwater supply were allocated per km2 based on population density
for each province. Per capita data for these variables were calculated by dividing the total
value by the population of each province, then distributed per km2 based on population density.
Groundwater exploitation rates were uniformly distributed across each province, with regions
having a population density below 1 person/km² assigned a rate of zero. Other factors were
allocated per km2 based on the resolution of raster data or vector data. Finally, groundwater
quality categories for each year and region were matched with the corresponding natural and
socio-economic variables to create the training and validation datasets for the RF model.”
7. Model Parameters and Tuning: The manuscript would benefit from a detailed description of the
random forest model parameters, including the settings for each parameter and the methods used
for tuning. If parameter optimization was conducted, please describe the process and the rationale
behind the chosen methods and settings.
Response: Thank you for your comment. In our modeling approach, we focused primarily on optimizing
the number of trees. We tested different values, increasing the number of trees in increments of 10,
ranging from 10 to 200. Through this process, we identified 50 trees as the optimal number, delivering
the highest model accuracy. To ensure the evaluation’s stability and reliability, we utilized 10-fold cross-
validation, which allowed us to evaluate performance across different data subsets, providing a robust
assessment and helping to mitigate the risk of overfitting.
Other hyperparameters of the RF model, such as the minimum leaf size for classification trees (set to 1),
were left at their default settings as provided by the MATLAB Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox.
These defaults are widely regarded as effective for many applications, and in some cases, the toolbox
enforces fixed values to prevent alteration. Given this, we did not find it necessary to adjust these
parameters further. Additionally, since we did not use a deep RF model, tree depth was not treated as a
tunable hyperparameter.
To enhance clarity, we have incorporated the following texts in the “Splitting the training and validation
sets” section of “Methods”:
“We began by optimizing the hyperparameters of the RF model, with a particular focus on the
number of decision trees. By systematically testing tree counts in increments of 10, from 10 to
200, we identified 50 trees as the optimal balance between accuracy and computational
efficiency (Fig. S21). Other parameters, such as minimum leaf size, were kept at their default
settings, as these have proven effective in similar applications.”

8. Uncertainty Analysis: An uncertainty analysis of the model results would be beneficial.
Providing an assessment of the model’s uncertainty will give readers a better understanding of the
reliability of the predictions.
Response: To evaluate the uncertainties of our model results, we conducted Monte Carlo simulations
using n=50 sets of randomized input data representing various uncertain future scenarios. This approach
enables us to quantify output uncertainty and highlight the range of possible outcomes and their
implications. By incorporating these uncertainty assessments, we offer a clearer understanding of
potential future groundwater quality under different conditions, providing policymakers with valuable
insights into associated risks.
We have detailed the steps and methods used for uncertainty analysis in “Methods”:
“Uncertainty analysis
To evaluate the impact of uncertainties in climate change, groundwater exploitation, and
pollution charge on model predictions, we applied Monte Carlo (MC) simulations to quantify
the variability in groundwater quality predictions due to input uncertainties76. This analysis
was conducted for the period 1980-2100, with data processed at 5-year intervals for 1980-
2015, annually from 2016 to 2020, and at 5-year intervals for future projections from 2025 to
2100 under four scenarios.
In each scenario-year combination, MC simulations with 50 members were run to introduce
variability in key natural and socio-economic predictors. Perturbations were applied to these
dominant factors, such as climate, groundwater exploitation and pollution charge, reflecting
their real-world uncertainties. For instance, temperature varied within a ±2°C range, while
predictors like precipitation, fertilizer, and pesticide use were perturbed by up to ±20%.
The results of these simulations can be used to evaluate the range of possible groundwater
quality outcomes based on uncertainties in input data. For each year and scenario, we
calculated the mean and standard deviation of the predicted probabilities based on the
ensemble outcomes, providing a robust estimate of both expectation and variability in
groundwater quality predictions.”
In addition, we have included an uncertainty analysis in “Discussion”:
“Although visual comparisons and statistical evaluations suggest that the model estimates are
generally reasonable, notable uncertainties remain. Monte Carlo simulations were applied to
assess uncertainties in PGQ probability predictions, providing insights into spatial and
temporal variability. As shown in Figs. S18(d-f) and S19(e-h), uncertainties are moderate
overall but higher in North and Northeast China from 1980 to 2100, likely due to complex
interactions between socio-economic factors and groundwater systems. Under Scenario IV,
uncertainties become more pronounced (Fig. S20), likely driven by increased discharges and
groundwater exploitation. This highlights the need for adaptive groundwater management and
pollution control strategies, particularly in high-emission scenarios, to mitigate adverse
impacts and enhance prediction reliability in vulnerable regions.”

10. Rationale for future scenario settings (L.497-514): The setting of future scenarios is crucial for
the interpretation of model results. Given that variables such as fertilizer and pesticide usage
appear to have a significant impact on the model, as indicated by Fig. S3 and the results section,
the rationale behind the high (3%), medium (1%), and low (-3%) annual change rates should be
discussed. This discussion could include the basis for these specific rates and how they align with
projected socio-economic and environmental trends.
Response:Thank you for your suggestion. The high (3%), medium (1%), and low (-3%) annual change
rates for groundwater exploitation and pollution discharge were established based on historical trends
and the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) framework. These rates were selected to strike a balance
between past trends and future projections, taking into account key factors such as industrial activities,
agricultural expansion, and environmental policies, as emphasized in relevant studies and SSP
assessments. In the revised manuscript, we have discussed the basis and limitations of our approach:
In the three scenarios, annual change rates of -3%, 1%, and 3% were assigned as gradients
for groundwater exploitation and pollution discharge, respectively. These rates were
determined based on historical trends69,70 and future projections71,72 related to industrial
activities, agricultural expansion, and environmental policies. The low rate of -3% reflects a
proactive approach toward reducing resource use and pollution discharge, aligning with the
sustainability-focused SSP1-1.9 scenario73. In contrast, the medium rate of 1% corresponds
to a moderate development pathway, as seen in SSP2-4.5. This scenario embodies a balanced
approach, allowing socio-economic development to progress while placing emphasis on
environmental protection74. The high rate of 3% aligns with the SSP5-8.5 scenario,
characterized by rapid economic growth and minimal environmental regulation75. This
scenario anticipates high energy demands, with significant reliance on fossil fuels and
industrial expansion. We acknowledge that future development may exhibit more intricate
patterns, and our current study may not fully capture this complexity and uncertainty. Then,
these rates were applied to the corresponding values from 2021 to 2100, and the cumulative
average was calculated as the model inputs in each year. Please refer to Table S5 for detailed
information on the specific scenario assumptions.”

5. Whether it is agricultural or industrial pollution, there is usually a lag time for it to migrate to
groundwater. The time can be several years or tens of years. How do you treat this in you study?
Response:Thank you for your insightful comment. In our study, we calculate cumulative average values

delayed migration of pollutants into groundwater. This approach enables our model to effectively capture
changes in groundwater quality over timescales of several years to decades.
In the revised manuscript, we have clarified this process:
“For other dynamic factors, their cumulative average values from 1980 to the target year were
calculated as the model inputs. This accounts for the lag in pollutant migration and effectively
captures the long-term impacts on groundwater quality.”

7. Is a kappa coefficient of 0.69 a bit low? Generally, we believe that a kappa coefficient higher
than 0.8 is best.
Response: Thank you for your insightful comment. While the kappa coefficient of 0.69 in our analysis
falls short of the ideal 0.80, it still reflects substantial agreement according to the standards set by
Landis and Koch (1977)25, who classified kappa values between 0.61 and 0.80 as indicating substantial
agreement. This is particularly significant given the inherent complexity and variability of environmental
data, which can affect classification consistency across different samples or contexts. As such, achieving
a kappa value above 0.8 is challenging in our study. In the revised manuscript, we have included the
following clarification:
“Additionally, the model achieves substantial agreement beyond chance in its classifications
with Cohen’s kappa coefficient of 0.69. While slightly below the ideal, this value falls within
0.61-0.80, which Landis and Koch (1977) defined as substantial agreement25. This slightly
lower kappa value reflects the inherent complexity and variability of the environmental data
and processes analyzed in this study.”

9. In the assessment of groundwater quality in lines 335-336, does the use of a single factor
assessment method make the results too pessimistic? Please explain.
Response: Thank you for your feedback. In our study, we adhere to the latest Chinese groundwater
quality standard (GB/T 14848-2017), which classifies overall groundwater quality based on the worst
indicator in the dataset. This approach closely aligns with the barrel theory, which asserts that the overall
performance or effectiveness of a system is limited by its weakest component, similar to how a barrel’s
capacity is determined by the height of its shortest stave. We acknowledge that this approach may lead
to more stringent assessments; however, it is crucial to ensure that all potential risks to groundwater
quality are thoroughly considered. Furthermore, by aligning with established standards, our results can
provide more targeted information for government agencies.
In the revised manuscript, we have added the following clarification to “Discussion”:
“Our single-factor assessment focuses on the worst indicator, which may lead to stricter
evaluations but offers a cautious approach to groundwater management.”
10. Since there is a lot of missing data before 1990, why not start the study directly from 1990?
Response: Thank you for your suggestion. It is indeed true that there is a significant amount of missing
data prior to 1990. Similar to our predictions for future groundwater quality, this study also aims to
reconstruct groundwater quality for the years preceding the range of our collected data. We have reliable
predictor variables available for the decade from 1980 to 1990, which makes this reconstruction feasible.
By including this earlier period, we can capture the historical evolution of groundwater conditions,
providing a more comprehensive assessment of water management policies over an extended timeline
and enhancing our understanding of long-term shifts in groundwater quality.
In the revised manuscript, we have added the following clarification in the “Calculation of the Affected
Population” section of “Methods”:
“The RF model was used to reconstruct and predict the spatiotemporal distribution of
groundwater quality from 1980 to 2100, enabling us to infer long-term trends in populations
potentially exposed to PGQ. We apply a probability cutoff (Prob ) of 0.5 to identify the

12. Line 337, when we evaluate the water quality, we usually think that the water above Class III
is beyond the standard. What is the basis for choosing Class V water as the boundary in this
manuscript?
Response: Thank you for your comment. We classify groundwater quality as poor or not poor using
Class V as the threshold, determining whether the water is suitable for drinking, with or without treatment.
According to the latest groundwater quality standards (GB/T 14848-2017), water in Classes I to IV is
considered fit for domestic drinking purposes, possibly with some treatment, whereas Class V water is
deemed unsuitable for such use. We recognize that applying Class III as a stricter boundary would
highlight more critical groundwater quality challenges. In the revised manuscript, we have added the
following clarification:
“Moreover, the use of Class V as a threshold for PGQ is conservative, and stricter thresholds
like Class IV could be considered.”
13. The spatial pattern of future land use is affected by both human activities and climate change.
In your article, you assume that the land use pattern of different scenarios is in 2020. Is this
assumption too arbitrary? Different scenarios of future land use are also available in the Qinghai-
Tibet Plateau database. Please explain why you don’t use them?
Response: Thank you for your valuable suggestion. In the revised manuscript, we have enhanced our
models to incorporate dynamic land use changes from 2020 to 2100 across various scenarios. This
improvement allows for more reasonable projections of groundwater quality changes in response to shifts
in land use patterns driven by human activities and climate change. To evaluate the impact of land use
change on groundwater quality, we have intentionally retained the 2020 baseline for Scenario Ⅰ, which
reflects our original results without accounting for future land use changes. This approach provides a
clear contrast between static and dynamic land use scenarios, enhancing both the interpretability and
practical relevance of our findings.
In the revised manuscript, we have included the following updates in the “Scenario settings” section and
the “Analysis of drivers” section of “Methods”,and revised the results for future scenarios accordingly:
Scenario settings:
“In Scenario I (Baseline), we assumed a consistent development intensity for all drivers.
Climate, groundwater exploitation, and pollution discharges were maintained at the same
levels as the cumulative average values in 2020. Similarly, land-use type in Scenario I was
also assumed to remain unchanged from 2020. In contrast, Scenarios II-IV incorporated
projections to account for future variability. Specifically, climate data from one CMIP6
model——EC-Earth3 were used as model input to project future PGQ probabilities65-67.
Additionally, land-use data in these scenarios were derived from the SSP-RCP global 1km
land-use simulation dataset (2020-2100) for SSP1-1.9, SSP2-4.5, and SSP5-8.5 scenarios,
updated every five years68. To maintain consistency in representation, these land-use data were
aligned with those used for the historical period from 1980 to 2020.
Analysis of drivers:
“In future scenarios, the analysis of dominant driver focuses exclusively on four primary
categories: climate change, groundwater exploitation, land use and pollution discharges,
without individually detailing secondary pollution categories. We kept one specific driver
category (e.g., climate) constant at its states in 2020, while allowing the other driver
categories to vary with time.”

14. The research conclusion should be summarized.
Response: Thank you for your suggestion. As the journal does not support including a “conclusion”
section in the article, we have incorporated a summary of the key findings and implications of our study
within the “Discussion” section, as follows:
“Despite the inherent limitations, our approach offers distinct advantages over traditional
methods, which are often labor-intensive and costly. By integrating regional data from
previous research with accessible natural and socio-economic predictors, our methodology
presents a comprehensive analytical framework for assessing groundwater qualities. This
strategy provides detailed patterns of groundwater quality evolution across China from 1980
to 2100, revealing that pollution discharge, groundwater over-exploitation, and land-use
change are significant contributors to its degradation, particularly in high-risk regions
affecting large populations. Furthermore, our projections indicate that proactive
environmental policies can substantially improve groundwater quality under diverse future
scenarios. This approach is especially valuable for developing countries, where limited
groundwater data and PGQ are common. By offering a cost-effective solution, our model not
only fills critical data gaps but also provides actionable insights into resource management
and strategic planning. Although uncertainties remain—especially regarding socio-economic
models and emissions paths—the findings underscore the need for adaptive, region-specific
groundwater management practices to mitigate socio-economic and climate-related impacts.
Future research can build on this model by refining data resolution and examining specific
pollutant pathways to enhance predictive reliability and support long-term, sustainable
groundwater policies.”
